chapter_title: Light Estimation and Anchors for Persistent AR

screens.title: Light Estimation and Anchors for Persistent AR
screens.subtitle: Make virtual objects match real light and stay fixed in place during an AR session

narration.text: In this lesson you will discover two essential techniques that make augmented objects feel part of the real world: light estimation and AR anchors. Light estimation uses the device camera to measure ambient intensity and color, and optionally dominant light direction and spherical harmonics. When you apply this data to your scene lighting, virtual objects pick up the room’s warmth, brightness, and shadows, which dramatically improves realism. AR Anchors solve a different problem: they provide a reliably tracked reference point so placed objects don’t drift as the device moves. You’ll learn how Unity’s AR Camera Manager exposes light estimates and how to apply those values to a Directional Light and ambient settings. You’ll also learn how the AR Anchor Manager creates anchors and how to parent placed content to anchors so they remain stable for the duration of a session. Together these features give you more believable visuals and stronger spatial stability. By the end you will be able to implement the example scripts and test them on a device to see lighting adapt and objects remain anchored. Think about a simple scene: a virtual lamp that takes on warm color in evening light, and a table model that stays precisely where you placed it even as you walk around—this lesson teaches those building blocks. What real object would you anchor first in your project?

keyIdea.title: Core insight
keyIdea.text: Use AR light estimation to adapt scene lighting and AR Anchors to keep objects stable inside a session; together they create more believable, persistent AR.

screens.subtitle: Skills you'll gain and why they matter

narration.text: By the end of this chapter you will understand how AR systems measure and expose lighting, and how to translate that data into scene lighting so virtual objects blend with real environments. You will implement a Unity script that listens for camera frame events and updates ambient and directional lighting parameters. You will also learn the purpose of AR Anchors and how to use the AR Anchor Manager to create and manage anchors so objects remain stable inside a session. Each objective ties a practical code step to a visual outcome: matching color temperature will make materials look warmer or cooler, adjusting intensity will change shadows and highlights, and anchoring will prevent slow drift. These skills matter because realism and stability are the two most visible signals a user uses to judge quality in an AR experience. You will practice by updating your AR Session Origin with AR Camera Manager and AR Anchor Manager, implementing the ARLightEstimator script, and modifying an ARPlacementManager to parent placed objects to anchors. screens.title: What is Light Estimation?
screens.subtitle: How AR platforms measure scene lighting and why it matters

narration.text: Light estimation is the process where the AR system analyses camera input to produce numeric representations of the scene’s lighting. Typical outputs include ambient intensity in lumens, average color or color temperature, and sometimes a main light direction or spherical harmonics probes used for global illumination approximations. In practice this means the platform provides values you can read each frame and use to alter your virtual scene so objects appear lit like the real world. For example, if a room is warm and dim, using the average color temperature to tint ambient light and lowering directional intensity makes a 3D model look less like a studio-lit prop and more like it belongs in that room. A common misconception is that light estimation will perfectly reproduce complex shadows and reflections; it won’t. It provides approximations that help materials and broad illumination match the environment. For reflective surfaces, spherical harmonics or additional probes give better approximations, but they remain estimates. A concrete example: you read averageIntensityInLumens from ARCameraManager frame data and divide it by a scale factor to set your scene’s directional light intensity. The immediate takeaway is that light estimation gives you measurable values to reduce the visual gap between physical and virtual content — not a perfect solution, but a powerful tool when paired with good materials and lighting setup.

keyIdea.title: Definition
keyIdea.text: Light estimation provides camera-derived measures like intensity and color temperature so virtual lighting can better match the real scene.

content.html:
Module 5 › Chapter 4.4 › What is Light Estimation?
Definition and value

Light estimation produces environmental lighting parameters from camera frames. These values let you adapt ambient and directional lighting so virtual objects match the scene’s tone.

Common outputs
  • averageIntensityInLumens — numeric overall brightness
  • averageColorTemperature or averageColor — color tint
  • mainLightDirection / mainLightIntensity — directional cues
  • spherical harmonics — for diffuse reflections
Why it matters
Matching light reduces the visual gap between real and virtual objects, increasing immersion and reducing the feeling of overlays.
Key Takeaway

Treat light estimation as guide values you apply to lighting components, not a full physical renderer replacement.

Concrete example
Imagine you place a virtual lamp in a dim cafe. If you set RenderSettings.ambientLight using the estimated color and lower the Directional Light intensity using averageIntensityInLumens, the lamp’s materials will pick up warm low light and softer shadows, blending into the cafe scene.
Misconception
Light estimation does not recreate detailed shadows or accurate reflections on glossy surfaces by itself; it supplies inputs to improve the overall impression.
Try this
On-device, toggle a Directional Light’s intensity using the reported lumens and watch shadow strength change as you move between bright and dim areas.

screens.title: AR Camera Manager and AR Light Estimation
screens.subtitle: How Unity exposes lighting data through frame events

narration.text: Unity’s AR Foundation exposes camera-derived lighting through the AR Camera Manager, which is usually added to your AR Session Origin. The AR Camera Manager raises a frameReceived event each time the AR subsystem has a new camera frame and associated metadata. That metadata can include a lightEstimation structure with values like averageIntensityInLumens, averageColorTemperature, and sometimes a mainLight direction or spherical harmonics probe. To use this, attach a component that subscribes to frameReceived and inspects the event argument’s lightEstimation property. You can either react to events or read updated values every frame. In practical terms, that means the camera acts as a sensor pipeline: it feeds measured lighting into your script so you can update RenderSettings. ambientLight or a Directional Light’s intensity and color. A typical architecture is: AR Session Origin contains AR Camera Manager and your ARLightEstimator component, and the scene contains a Directional Light and your materials. The ARLightEstimator maps numeric estimates to Unity lighting properties, sometimes scaling or smoothing values to avoid abrupt jumps. A common pitfall is updating light properties with raw values directly; you should clamp and smooth changes over several frames to reduce flicker. When you follow this pattern, your virtual objects will adapt continuously to environmental changes, producing a much more convincing AR experience.

keyIdea.title: Architecture
keyIdea.text: AR Camera Manager emits frame events containing light estimates; subscribe and map those values to scene lighting with smoothing to avoid flicker.

content.html:
Module 5 › Chapter 4.4 › AR Camera Manager
Component flow
AR Camera Manager → frameReceived event → your estimator script → update lights and probes.
Event data
  • averageIntensityInLumens
  • averageColorTemperature or averageColor
  • mainLightDirection and mainLightIntensity (optional)
  • sphericalHarmonics (for advanced lighting)
Best practice
Smooth changes over frames, clamp extreme values, and test on real devices under varying conditions to tune scale factors.
Visualization
Scene mapping
Use directional light for the main source and RenderSettings.ambientLight for general tone. Optionally update custom probes with spherical harmonics for reflections.
Common mistake
Applying raw intensity without scaling makes objects too bright or too dark. Use a divisor or curve to map lumens to Unity intensity nicely.
Key Takeaway

AR Camera Manager supplies the raw lighting inputs; your script interprets and smooths them for scene use.

screens.title: Implementing ARLightEstimator
screens.subtitle: Subscribe to frame events and update ambient and directional light

narration.text: Now we’ll walk through a concrete script pattern for applying ambient and directional lighting estimates. The ARLightEstimator component subscribes to AR Camera Manager’s frameReceived event in OnEnable and unsubscribes in OnDisable. Inside the frame callback you check whether eventArgs. lightEstimation contains values; if averageColorTemperature is present use it to tint RenderSettings. ambientLight, and if averageIntensityInLumens is present adjust your Directional Light’s intensity after scaling it down so values map to Unity units sensibly. Attach this script to AR Session Origin or a GameObject that has AR Camera Manager. A practical tip: prefer FindObjectOfType to get the directional light only for small scenes; in larger projects expose the Light as a serialized reference to avoid runtime cost. Smoothing is important—interpolate between the previous and new intensity to avoid flicker when camera exposure fluctuates. A concrete example: divide the reported lumens by 1000 and then lerp the scene light’s intensity over 0.1 seconds to make a smooth transition. Finally, remember that not every device provides the same fields; always check HasValue before using a property. This approach turns camera measurements into gradual, believable lighting changes in your AR scene.

keyIdea.title: Pattern
keyIdea.text: Subscribe to frameReceived, check lightEstimation values safely, map and scale them, and smooth updates to lighting properties.

content.html:
Module 5 › Chapter 4.4 › ARLightEstimator Code
Code Walkthrough

This example subscribes to frameReceived and sets ambient and directional lighting using safe HasValue checks and scaling.

using UnityEngine;
using UnityEngine.XR.ARFoundation;
using UnityEngine.XR.ARSubsystems;

public class ARLightEstimator : MonoBehaviour
{
    private ARCameraManager arCameraManager;

    void Awake()
    {
        arCameraManager = GetComponent<ARCameraManager>();
    }

    void OnEnable()
    {
        arCameraManager.frameReceived += OnCameraFrameReceived;
    }

    void OnDisable()
    {
        arCameraManager.frameReceived -= OnCameraFrameReceived;
    }

    void OnCameraFrameReceived(ARCameraFrameEventArgs eventArgs)
    {
        if (eventArgs.lightEstimation.averageColorTemperature.HasValue)
        {
            RenderSettings.ambientLight = Color.white; // Map color temp to a Color in practice
        }

        if (eventArgs.lightEstimation.averageIntensityInLumens.HasValue)
        {
            Light sceneLight = FindObjectOfType<Light>();
            if (sceneLight != null && sceneLight.type == LightType.Directional)
            {
                sceneLight.intensity = eventArgs.lightEstimation.averageIntensityInLumens.Value / 1000f; 
            }
        }
    }
}
Explanation & Tips
  • Always check HasValue before using light estimation fields.
  • Scale lumens to a Unity-friendly range; typical divisor values vary per scene.
  • Cache scene references and avoid heavy calls inside every frame callback.
  • Smooth updates with Lerp to avoid abrupt lighting changes.
Pro tip
Expose your Directional Light via inspector instead of using FindObjectOfType for better performance and reliability.
Key Takeaway

Use frame events to drive lighting but map and smooth values so the scene changes are believable and stable.

screens.title: What are AR Anchors?
screens.subtitle: Anchors as the foundation for persistent and stable placement

narration.text: An AR Anchor is a tracked reference point in the real world that the AR subsystem continuously refines and maintains. When you create an anchor at a particular pose and parent a virtual object to that anchor’s transform, the underlying platform works to keep that transform aligned with real-world features as the device moves. This reduces drift and wobble that often reveal virtual objects as overlays rather than part of the scene. Anchors are essential for any experience that relies on consistent object placement over time in a single session — for example, keeping a virtual chair on your living room floor as you walk around it, or fixing a painting to a wall so multiple viewers see it at the same spot. A key limitation is that anchors are session-scoped by default: if the app closes or tracking fails completely, anchors may lose alignment or need to be re-established. Achieving cross-session persistence requires storing anchor data and re-resolving it later, which often involves cloud services or platform-specific persistence APIs. For most beginner projects, anchors provide a robust way to keep content stable during active use. When placing anchors, consider creating them only when tracking confidence is high to avoid saving inaccurate reference points.

keyIdea.title: Anchor role
keyIdea.text: AR Anchors are session-tracked reference points you parent objects to in order to minimize drift and keep placements stable.

content.html:
Module 5 › Chapter 4.4 › What are AR Anchors?
Anchor definition

An anchor is a fixed real-world point tracked by the AR system. Parent your virtual object to an ARAnchor so the system maintains its alignment as tracking updates.

Why use anchors
They significantly reduce drift, improving perceived stability for placed content during an active session.
When to prefer anchors
When objects must remain at a specific real-world location or when multi-touch positioning requires reliable transforms.
Limitations & considerations
  • Anchors are generally session-scoped unless you implement persistence externally.
  • Anchors depend on underlying tracking quality; full loss of tracking can invalidate them.
  • Create anchors only when tracking confidence is good to avoid bad saved poses.
Common misconception
Anchors do not guarantee perfect absolute world alignment across app restarts without additional persistence steps.
Key Takeaway

Use anchors to improve placement stability during sessions; treat cross-session persistence as an advanced follow-up task.

screens.title: Using AR Anchor Manager in Unity
screens.subtitle: Create, remove, and parent objects to anchors

narration.text: Unity provides an AR Anchor Manager component you add to AR Session Origin to create and maintain anchors. Programmatically, call arAnchorManager. AddAnchor(pose) to obtain an ARAnchor. The returned ARAnchor has a transform you can parent your placed object to so the AR system updates that transform as it refines tracking. In practice, when a user taps the screen and a raycast hits a plane, you create an anchor at the hit pose and instantiate your object as a child of the anchor. If you move the object later, remove the old anchor with arAnchorManager. RemoveAnchor and create a new one at the new pose, re-parenting the object so its transform is managed by the new anchor. This pattern gives a reliable lifecycle: anchors are created at placement, used to stabilize content, and removed when the content moves or is deleted. Always check for null returns from AddAnchor — if the anchor cannot be created, fall back to placing the object without an anchor or notify the user. Also consider cleaning up anchors when scenes unload to avoid orphaned references. These steps make object placement more robust and user-friendly in real AR sessions.

keyIdea.title: Anchor workflow
keyIdea.text: Use ARAnchorManager.AddAnchor to create anchors at poses, parent objects to them, and remove anchors when moving or deleting objects.

content.html:
Module 5 › Chapter 4.4 › AR Anchor Manager
Placement lifecycle
  1. Raycast to find hit pose on a plane.
  2. Call arAnchorManager.AddAnchor(hitPose).
  3. Instantiate or parent object to the returned ARAnchor transform.
  4. On move, remove old anchor and create a new one.
Edge case
AddAnchor can fail if tracking is not ready. Always null-check and provide a fallback placement strategy.
Example integration
Below is the ARPlacementManager example modified to use ARAnchorManager. It demonstrates creating an anchor and parenting the placed object, including anchor removal when relocating the object.
using UnityEngine;
using UnityEngine.XR.ARFoundation;
using UnityEngine.XR.ARSubsystems;
using System.Collections.Generic;

public class ARPlacementManager : MonoBehaviour
{
    [SerializeField] private GameObject objectToPlace;
    private ARRaycastManager arRaycastManager;
    private ARAnchorManager arAnchorManager;
    private static List<ARRaycastHit> hits = new List<ARRaycastHit>();

    private GameObject placedObject;
    private ARAnchor placedObjectAnchor;

    void Awake()
    {
        arRaycastManager = GetComponent<ARRaycastManager>();
        arAnchorManager = GetComponent<ARAnchorManager>();
    }

    void Update()
    {
        if (Input.touchCount > 0)
        {
            Touch touch = Input.GetTouch(0);
            if (touch.phase == TouchPhase.Began)
            {
                if (arRaycastManager.Raycast(touch.position, hits, TrackableType.PlaneWithinPolygon))
                {
                    Pose hitPose = hits[0].pose;

                    if (placedObject == null)
                    {
                        placedObjectAnchor = arAnchorManager.AddAnchor(hitPose);
                        if (placedObjectAnchor != null)
                        {
                            placedObject = Instantiate(objectToPlace, placedObjectAnchor.transform);
                            placedObject.transform.localPosition = Vector3.zero;
                            placedObject.transform.localRotation = Quaternion.identity;
                        }
                    }
                    else
                    {
                        if (placedObjectAnchor != null)
                        {
                            arAnchorManager.RemoveAnchor(placedObjectAnchor);
                        }
                        placedObjectAnchor = arAnchorManager.AddAnchor(hitPose);
                        if (placedObjectAnchor != null)
                        {
                            placedObject.transform.SetParent(placedObjectAnchor.transform);
                            placedObject.transform.localPosition = Vector3.zero;
                            placedObject.transform.localRotation = Quaternion.identity;
                        }
                    }
                }
            }
        }
    }
}
Key Takeaway

Anchors should be created at confirmed hit poses and removed when relocating content to maintain a clean anchor lifecycle.

screens.title: Anchored Placement vs Simple Transform Updates
screens.subtitle: Why parenting to anchors improves stability over direct transforms

narration.text: There are two common ways to place objects in AR: directly set a GameObject’s transform to a hit pose, or create an ARAnchor and parent the object to it. Direct transform updates are inexpensive and straightforward, and they work well for transient or purely local visuals. However, as the AR system refines its understanding of the environment, direct transforms do not receive continuous correction from the tracking subsystem and can slowly drift. Anchors, by contrast, are integrated into the tracking lifecycle. When you create an ARAnchor, the AR subsystem maintains the anchor’s transform and actively corrects it based on feature tracking. Parenting your content to that anchor transfers those corrections to your object. In practice you will notice anchored objects remain fixed relative to real-world features while direct-transform objects show subtle shifts over time. A useful heuristic is: use anchors when you need multi-frame stability or when users will move around the object; use direct transforms for ephemeral visuals that do not need long-term spatial fidelity. A common misconception is that anchors are always heavier to manage — they add some lifecycle management, but for persistent placements the trade-off is almost always worth it to avoid drift.

keyIdea.title: Comparison
keyIdea.text: Anchors provide continuous tracking corrections for stability; direct transforms are simpler but prone to drift over time.

content.html:
Module 5 › Chapter 4.4 › Anchored vs Direct
Direct Transform Placement
Set the GameObject.transform.position and rotation to the raycast hit pose. Quick and simple for short-lived content.
  • Pros: minimal lifecycle code, lower overhead.
  • Cons: object can drift as tracking evolves.
When to use
HUD elements, temporary markers, or quick previews.
Anchor-based Placement
Create an ARAnchor at the hit pose and parent the object to the anchor’s transform so the AR system maintains alignment.
  • Pros: improved stability and persistence during session.
  • Cons: requires anchor lifecycle management and null checks.
When to use
Any object that should remain at a specific real-world location while users move around it.
Misconception check

Anchors don't guarantee persistence across app restarts; they improve stability within the current tracking session.

screens.title: Hands-on Activity: Integrate Light Estimation and Anchors
screens.subtitle: Step-by-step implementation checklist based on the chapter activity

narration.text: Follow this step-by-step checklist to integrate light estimation and anchors into your existing project. Start from your Chapter 4.3 project. First, add ARCameraManager to your AR Session Origin if it isn’t present; this exposes frame events with lightEstimation. Second, create the ARLightEstimator script, attach it to the AR Session Origin, and ensure it subscribes to frameReceived to update ambient and directional light. Test by moving between a bright area and a dim area and observe changes. Third, add ARAnchorManager to AR Session Origin to enable anchor creation APIs. Fourth, modify ARPlacementManager to use ARAnchorManager. AddAnchor when placing objects, and parent placed objects to the created ARAnchor. When moving objects, remove the old anchor and add a new one. Fifth, build and run on a physical device—this is crucial because lighting and tracking are device dependent. Observe the placed cube: it should adapt its lighting and remain stable as you walk around. A common pitfall during the activity is forgetting to check HasValue for light fields or not smoothing intensity changes, producing flicker. Another is not null-checking the AddAnchor return which can lead to null references. Work through each step, verify behavior, and iterate until lighting and placement feel natural.

screens.title: Advanced Lighting: Spherical Harmonics & Reflections
screens.subtitle: When to apply probes and harmonic data for improved realism

narration.text: For surfaces that respond to indirect light and reflections, simple ambient color and a Directional Light may not be enough. Some AR platforms provide spherical harmonics or environment probe data that approximate how light arrives from many directions. Spherical harmonics are compact representations of the diffuse light field and are useful for shading materials that need softer, multi-directional illumination. In Unity, if the AR subsystem exposes spherical harmonics, you can use that data to update a custom lighting probe or shader property so your materials respond to ambient directionality. This is particularly helpful for matte surfaces and diffuse interreflections where the overall tone and subtle directional variation matter. Reflective and glossy surfaces also benefit from environment probes that capture a low-resolution cubemap; those cubemaps can be used for reflections or as a source for specular highlights. A practical limitation is that these advanced data types can be heavier to compute and apply, and not every device or platform shares them. A common misconception is that spherical harmonics give perfect reflections; instead, they provide an efficient approximation for broad diffuse lighting and should be complemented by other techniques for high-fidelity specular reflections. Use these tools when you need extra realism and when performance budgets permit.

keyIdea.title: Advanced shading
keyIdea.text: Spherical harmonics and environment probes improve diffuse and reflective lighting approximations but require more work and are not always available on all devices.

content.html:
Module 5 › Chapter 4.4 › Spherical Harmonics
What spherical harmonics do

They encode multi-directional diffuse light into compact coefficients that shaders can use to approximate indirect illumination across a surface.

Use cases
Matt surfaces, soft ambient shading, and improving perceived depth for objects in complex lighting.
Limitations
Not a substitute for high-quality reflections or dynamic specular lighting; availability varies between platforms.
Practical steps
  1. Check whether lightEstimation exposes sphericalHarmonicsCoefficients.
  2. Convert those coefficients into a form your shader or probe accepts.
  3. Update a reflection probe or shader parameters on new data and smooth changes.
Performance note
Updating harmonics every frame can be expensive. Consider updating at lower frequency or when changes exceed a threshold.
Key Takeaway

Use spherical harmonics and probes to improve diffuse lighting fidelity, but balance accuracy with performance and platform support.

screens.title: Common Mistakes and Troubleshooting
screens.subtitle: Avoid flicker, null references, and poor anchor placement

narration.text: When implementing light estimation and anchors you will encounter a handful of recurring issues. First, flicker from raw camera-exposed values is common if you set lighting properties with no smoothing. Remedy this by interpolating intensity and color over a few frames. Second, null references from AddAnchor failing or from missing Directional Light references occur frequently; always null-check and expose required objects through the inspector for predictable behavior. Third, incorrect anchor placement can happen if you create anchors while tracking confidence is low or if the hit pose is noisy; avoid creating anchors until the raycast result and tracking state are stable. Fourth, forgetting to clean up anchors when removing objects can leave unused anchors in the scene; ensure RemoveAnchor is called when objects are deleted or moved. Fifth, platform variability means not all devices supply the same light fields; guard code paths and degrade gracefully when certain fields are absent. Finally, test on-device in multiple lighting conditions and physically move around placed content to observe real behavior. These checks and practices reduce crashes and make your AR scenes feel polished and reliable to users.

keyIdea.title: Troubleshooting
keyIdea.text: Smooth values, check for nulls, avoid premature anchor creation, and clean up anchors to prevent drift and errors.

content.html:
Module 5 › Chapter 4.4 › Troubleshooting
Common mistakes
Flicker
Interpolate light values instead of applying raw numbers each frame.
Null references
Always check for null when using AddAnchor and FindObjectOfType; expose references via inspector where possible.
Bad anchor placement
Create anchors only when tracking confidence and hit results are reliable to avoid storing noisy poses.
Clean up anchors
Remove anchors when objects are deleted or moved to prevent stray anchors and keep the scene tidy.
Test broadly
Run tests in different rooms and lighting to tune scaling factors and smoothing durations for robust behavior.
Key Takeaway

Guard inputs, smooth outputs, and manage anchor lifecycles to produce reliable AR behaviour.

screens.title: Build, Run, and Observe — Practical Deployment Tips
screens.subtitle: Why device testing is essential and what to look for in results

narration.text: The final step is to build and run on a physical device. Emulators cannot fully replicate camera exposure, real lighting variation, or true tracking behavior. When you deploy to a device, observe three things. First, watch how ambient color and intensity values change as you move between different lit areas, and see whether your virtual materials respond smoothly. If colors jump or flicker, increase smoothing or lower update frequency. Second, place an object and walk around it; anchored objects should remain aligned to the same real-world feature while direct transforms may slowly drift. If anchors drift, check tracking quality and ensure anchors were created when tracking confidence was high. Third, test edge cases: sudden lighting changes, occlusion by objects, and rapid device motion. Each test reveals different weaknesses in lighting mapping or anchor robustness. Keep logs or on-screen debug text to capture reported lightEstimation values while testing — these numbers help you tune mapping factors. The practical insight is that iterative device testing and tuning is where the theoretical benefits of light estimation and anchors become apparent; small code changes yield visible improvements only when validated under real conditions.

keyIdea.title: Deploy wisely
keyIdea.text: Test lighting adaption and anchor stability on physical devices, iterate smoothing and scaling, and verify behavior under varied conditions.

content.html:
Module 5 › Chapter 4.4 › Build & Run
Device testing checklist
Lighting observation
Confirm ambient tint and intensity adjust as you move through lit and dim areas.
Anchor stability
Place objects, walk around, and verify they remain aligned to the same real-world spot.
Edge cases
Test sudden lighting changes, occlusion, and rapid motion to reveal weak points.
Add a small on-screen debug panel that prints reported averageIntensityInLumens and averageColorTemperature so you can tune mapping factors quickly while observing the scene. Device testing will guide practical choices like update frequency and smoothing time constants.
Key Takeaway

Real device testing is mandatory; visual improvements and anchor reliability are visible only under real lighting and motion conditions.

narration.text: Here are the compact concepts to carry forward. First, light estimation provides numeric camera-derived values—intensity, color temperature, and sometimes main light direction or spherical harmonics—that you can map to Unity lighting to improve realism. Second, AR Camera Manager is the primary Unity component that exposes frame events and lightEstimation data; subscribe and read these values safely. Third, AR Anchors are tracked reference points created with AR Anchor Manager; parent placed objects to anchors to reduce drift and increase stability during a session. Each of these concepts has practical caveats: scale and smooth light values to avoid flicker; always null-check or verify HasValue before use; and understand that anchors are session-scoped unless you implement persistence. Together these techniques produce AR experiences with stronger believability and more stable placements. Use the scripts and workflow demonstrated in the chapter as a reliable starting point for real-device iteration and refinement.

screens.title: What to Remember
screens.subtitle: Three compact cards to carry into your next AR build

narration.text: Keep three compact rules in mind as you build AR experiences. First, treat light estimation as an input stream—read values, scale them into Unity’s lighting ranges, and smooth updates before applying them. Second, use AR Anchors for any content that must remain in a fixed real-world location during a session; create anchors at reliable hit poses and parent your objects. Third, always test on a physical device under varied lighting and motion to tune scaling, smoothing, and placement thresholds. These practices reduce visible artifacts like flicker and drift and make virtual content convincingly part of the scene. They also prepare you for more advanced steps, like saving anchor data for cross-session persistence later. Carry these three priorities—scale and smooth lighting, anchor lifetime management, and real-device iteration—into your next feature, and you’ll notice immediate quality improvements.
